ami_style_notes: The conversational style of this meeting is notably bifurcated: the pre-seminar small talk operates at a very casual, short-turn register with frequent back-channeling ("yeah," "right," "oh no," "wow wow"), while the formal presentation segments shift to long, uninterrupted monologue stretches with complex nested clause structures. Formality is low to moderate throughout — even the scientific Q&A retains informal hedges like "I mean," "sort of," "you know," and "I guess," and speakers routinely soften claims with phrases such as "what we think is going on," "it could be possible that," "I would never try to convince you of that," and "these are all questions we're interested in." False starts and self-corrections are common ("the — so — the first thing," "and — and — and"), and speakers frequently repeat words or short phrases for emphasis or as a stalling mechanism ("very very very different," "I I I I"). Disagreement is almost entirely indirect, expressed through reframing or gentle qualification rather than direct challenge, and questions in the Q&A are routinely preceded by self-deprecating framing ("I have a naive question," "I'll be the first to admit"). Participants build on each other cooperatively, often echoing the previous speaker's phrasing before pivoting. Interruptions are rare during formal segments but light overlapping affirmations ("yeah," "right," "okay") are constant in casual exchanges. Filler words — "uh," "um," "so," "basically," "again," "sort of" — appear at high frequency across both registers, giving even the technical passages a spontaneous, thinking-aloud quality.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Renata Osei
speakers.background: Renata completed her PhD in social epidemiology four years ago, focusing on neighborhood-level determinants of cardiovascular disease in urban populations. She spent two years at a school of public health running community health surveys before joining this project. Her methodological toolkit centers on prospective cohort designs, validated psychiatric screening instruments like the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, and GIS-based spatial analysis for quantifying green space access. She is accustomed to translating messy social realities into measurable, reproducible variables, but has grown privately uncertain about whether standard epidemiological operationalizations fully capture the lived experience of mental health in communities shaped by structural racism and disinvestment.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Renata sees the research problem as fundamentally about establishing a defensible causal pathway: does proximity to and use of green space reduce the incidence or severity of depression and anxiety, and if so, by how much, in whom, and under what conditions? She wants to pin down the exposure variable — measurable park access, acreage, quality indices — and link it to validated outcome measures collected at baseline and follow-up. Her uncertainty surfaces when she tries to decide whether standard definitions of 'green space access' or 'depression' are appropriate for communities whose relationship to public space has been shaped by histories of exclusion and policing. She worries that the instruments she trusts most may be measuring something slightly different in this context, but she doesn't yet have a clear methodological answer for that concern.

speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Lind
speakers.background: Marcus trained originally as a civil engineer before pivoting to STS, where he earned his doctorate examining how urban planning technologies — zoning maps, green infrastructure metrics, park quality indices — encode particular assumptions about who cities are built for. He has spent the last eight years doing ethnographic and document-analysis work embedded in city planning departments and public health agencies, watching how data collection tools shape the phenomena they claim to measure. He joined this project specifically because he believes that the categories epidemiologists use to study green space and mental health are themselves political artifacts worth interrogating, not neutral containers waiting to be filled with observations.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Marcus approaches the research problem by asking who defined 'green space,' who defined 'mental health,' and what those definitional choices do in practice. For him, the key issue is not whether the study can isolate a clean exposure-outcome relationship, but rather how the act of measuring — choosing instruments, drawing boundaries, assigning diagnoses — participates in constructing the very realities it purports to observe. He is genuinely excited about the mixed-methods design because he sees qualitative data as an opportunity to surface how residents themselves understand and contest categories like 'park access' or 'anxiety.' He is confident that STS thinking is indispensable here, and he tends to push hard on conceptual foundations before worrying about operational details, which puts him in recurring friction with Renata's drive toward instrument finalization.

epidemiology.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
epidemiology.definition: In epidemiology, 'exposure' refers to contact with a factor (in this case, proximity to or use of urban green space) that may causally influence a health outcome. It is a measurable, quantifiable variable — typically operationalized as dose, duration, or frequency — used in cohort or case-control studies to assess risk or benefit. For example, 'green space exposure' might be defined as living within 300 meters of a park or spending at least 30 minutes per week in a green area.
epidemiology.example_usage_in_context: Dr. Osei uses 'exposure' when discussing how to measure residents' contact with green space as an independent variable in their prospective cohort study.

science_and_technology_studies.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
science_and_technology_studies.definition: In STS, 'exposure' often refers to the political and social process by which hidden, suppressed, or taken-for-granted assumptions, power relations, or knowledge-making practices are revealed and made visible — particularly how marginalized communities are rendered legible or vulnerable to institutional scrutiny. 'Exposure' can carry a critical, even cautionary connotation: it may refer to the act of uncovering who defines a problem, whose knowledge counts, or how communities are subjected to classification and measurement by outside researchers.
science_and_technology_studies.example_usage_in_context: Dr. Lind uses 'exposure' when raising concerns about the research process itself — specifically about how the act of studying low-income communities through epidemiological frameworks exposes those communities to particular forms of institutional gaze and categorization.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Okay, so — thanks for making time for this, Marcus. I know we're both sort of buried right now. I want to make sure we actually leave today with something concrete, because the IRB deadline is coming up faster than I'd like and I need the instruments finalized. So, um, maybe we just start with the exposure variable, because I think that's where our frameworks might be pulling in different directions. My instinct is to operationalize it as — you know — living within 300 meters of a park, plus a self-reported measure of time spent there per week, something like 30 minutes or more. That gives me a quantifiable, consistent definition I can apply across the whole cohort. But I'm genuinely uncertain whether that definition is actually capturing what matters for the communities we're working in. So I guess my question for you is — from where you're sitting, does that operationalization make sense, or are there dimensions of how residents actually relate to these spaces that you think it's missing? And if so, what would you actually want us to add or change in the instrument?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: Yeah, so — I really appreciate you framing it that way, asking what's missing, because that's exactly where I want to start. And I think your instinct that something might be off is worth following. The 300-meter buffer and the time-spent measure — those are reasonable starting points, I'm not saying throw them out. But here's the thing I keep coming back to: a park within 300 meters isn't the same as a park someone actually feels safe going to, or welcome in, or like the space was built with them in mind. And those distinctions matter a lot for whether being physically proximate to green space actually does anything for mental health. I mean, there's a really important question buried in there about what 'access' even means. A resident can live right next to a park and experience it as — I don't know — a space that's policed heavily, or that caters to a different demographic, or that simply doesn't feel like theirs. That's a very very different relationship to the exposure than the one the 300-meter measure assumes. So I guess what I'd push for — and this is where I think the qualitative arm can actually do real work before we lock in the instruments — is letting residents tell us what they think access means, what park use looks like for them, before we finalize the quantitative definition. Because right now we're essentially importing a definition that was built for a different context and applying it here, and I want us to at least be honest with ourselves about that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Yeah, I mean — I think you're right, and honestly that's the worry I keep circling back to too. The 300-meter buffer is a GIS artifact, basically. It doesn't know anything about how a space feels to the person who lives near it. So I'm with you on that. The thing I'm stuck on is — okay, so how do we actually move that insight into the instrument before the IRB deadline? Like, concretely. Because I can't submit 'let residents define access' as my exposure variable — I need something measurable and consistent across, what, 400 participants. So here's what I'm wondering: could we add a small set of questions right alongside the time-spent measure — things like, do you feel safe in this space, do you feel like it's for people like you, have you avoided it because of police presence or something like that? That wouldn't be perfect, but it would at least flag whether proximity and felt access are diverging for a given respondent. And then the qualitative arm could go deeper on the why. Does that seem like it would address what you're describing, or am I still flattening it too much?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: Yeah, that — that's actually a really good move, and I want to say yes to it clearly, because I think that's the right direction. Adding those questions — safety, belonging, police presence — that starts to crack open what access actually means in practice. So yes, let's do that. I'd push for framing them carefully though, because 'do you feel like it's for people like you' is doing a lot of work in a single question, and I think we can be more specific. Like, we could ask whether they've seen their neighbors using the space, whether their kids go there, whether they've ever been approached by security or police while using it. Those are all things residents can answer concretely, and together they give you a texture that 'time spent' alone doesn't. And the reason I care about that specificity is — this is kind of a foundational thing for me — the way we phrase those questions is itself a choice about whose experience we're treating as the default. If we ask 'do you feel safe' with no context, we're assuming the respondent knows what we mean by safe, and whose standard of safety we're measuring against. So getting that language right matters, not just for validity in the technical sense, but because it signals to participants whether this study actually sees them. Which — I mean, that's also a retention issue, practically speaking, so Renata that's not just me being philosophical. And then yes, the qualitative work goes deeper on the why behind whatever patterns the survey surfaces. But I'd actually argue we should do a small round of cognitive interviews with residents before IRB submission — even five or six conversations — just to stress-test whether those added questions mean what we think they mean to the people answering them. That's not a huge ask in terms of time, and it would make the whole instrument more defensible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Okay, the cognitive interviews — I actually think that's a really good idea, and honestly I'm kicking myself a little for not building that in from the start. Five or six conversations before we finalize is doable, especially if we're strategic about who we recruit for that. And you're right that it makes the instrument more defensible to a reviewer, not just more valid in practice. So let's put that in the plan. What I want to make sure is that we're treating it as an instrument refinement step with a clear endpoint — meaning we do the interviews, we adjust the language on those added questions based on what we hear, and then we lock the instrument. I don't want it to become an open-ended process that pushes the IRB submission by two months. So I guess what I'd want us to agree on today is: who conducts those interviews, what's the specific list of questions we're stress-testing, and what's our decision rule for when a question is 'close enough' versus needs to be rewritten. On the question framing — I hear you on 'do you feel like it's for people like you' being too vague. The more concrete alternatives you're suggesting, the neighbor use, kids going there, police contact, those feel much more answerable and they're also things I can code consistently across respondents. So I'd rather build it that way. The one thing I want to flag is that we still need a way to aggregate those items into something I can include as a covariate in the model. So either they form a small scale, or I treat them as separate moderators. That's a decision I need to make before submission too. Can we work through that today?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: Yeah, let's work through that — and I think the aggregation question is actually more tractable than it might feel right now. My instinct is that you probably don't want to collapse those items into a single scale, because what you'd lose is the ability to see whether it's safety that's doing the work, or police presence specifically, or belonging. Those might have very different relationships to the mental health outcomes, and if you average them together you'd never know. So I'd lean toward treating them as separate moderators — or at minimum, running the analysis both ways and seeing if the picture changes. That's a decision you can make after the cognitive interviews, because you might find that two of the items are basically synonymous in how people respond to them, and then collapsing those two makes sense. So I don't think we have to fully resolve it today — we just need to agree that we're not forcing them into a single index before we know whether they're measuring the same thing. On the process questions — who conducts the interviews, decision rules — I think those are genuinely easy to sort out. I'd want to be involved in at least some of the interviews, or at least in analyzing what we hear, because I think that's where the conceptual work happens. But you or a RA could run them with a simple protocol. And the decision rule could be pretty straightforward: if more than, say, two out of six respondents interpret a question in a way that diverges from what we intended, the question gets rewritten. That gives us a clear threshold without making it open-ended. Does that feel workable to you?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Yeah, that threshold feels workable — two out of six is clear, it's not too strict, and it gives us an exit criterion. Okay, so let's call that settled: that's our decision rule. And I'm actually reassured by what you said about the aggregation question, because I think you're right that collapsing them too early would cost us information. So — provisional plan is we treat them as separate moderators in the primary analysis, we keep the option open to collapse any items that turn out to be redundant based on what the cognitive interviews surface, and I note that flexibility in the statistical analysis plan when I write it up. That's something I can defend to a reviewer. The one thing I still want to nail down before we end today is — which specific items are we taking into the cognitive interviews? So, the neighbor use question, kids going there, police contact — I'm on board with those three. Are there others you'd add? Because I want us to have an actual list, like five to eight items max, that we're testing. Otherwise 'stress-test the instrument' stays abstract and we'll be relitigating this in two weeks when we're trying to write the interview protocol.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: Right, okay, let me just — let me try to give you a concrete list right now, because you're right, we need to pin this down. So I'd keep the three you named — neighbor use, kids going there, police or security contact — and then I'd add a few more. One would be something like: have you ever gone to the park and left earlier than you intended because of how you felt there? That's a behavioral trace of the belonging question without asking about belonging directly. Another one: is there a time of day when you avoid the space, and if so, why? That captures both safety and maybe scheduling constraints that are specific to low-income residents — work hours, caregiving — which is actually a dimension the 300-meter buffer completely ignores. And then I'd want one question that gets at whether the park feels maintained or cared for in a way that signals who it's for — something like, does this space look like it gets the same upkeep as parks in other parts of the city. That one's a little more interpretive, which is exactly why it needs cognitive testing, because I want to know whether residents read it the way we intend. So that gives you six items — three of yours, three of mine. I could maybe argue for one more on displacement, like whether they've noticed the space changing in recent years in ways that feel like it's catering to different people. That's relevant in any neighborhood where there's even low-level gentrification pressure. But if you want to cap it at six to keep the cognitive interviews tight, I can live with dropping that last one.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Okay, so that gives us six solid items and I think we can work with that. The one about leaving the park earlier than intended — I really like that one, actually, because it's behavioral, it's concrete, it's not asking someone to rate a feeling on a scale. The time-of-day question is good too, though I want to flag that when we write the protocol we'll need to be careful not to let it sprawl into a whole conversation about work schedules — we want a quick, codeable answer. The upkeep question I'm a little less certain about, not because I think it's wrong, but because I'm not sure residents will have a comparison point for 'parks in other parts of the city.' Like, if someone has rarely left their neighborhood, that comparison might not land. So let's put that one on the list as a question mark — we test it and if more than two respondents are confused by it, we rewrite or drop it. That's exactly what the cognitive interviews are for. On the displacement item — honestly, I'd keep it in. It's only one more question and gentrification is real in these neighborhoods. We can add it and flag it as exploratory. So let's call it seven items. What I want to do before we close today is just confirm who's writing the first draft of the cognitive interview protocol. I can have someone do a rough draft by end of next week if you can review it the week after. Does that timeline work for you?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: Yeah, that timeline works — end of next week for the draft, I'll review the week after, that's fine. And I'm glad we're keeping the displacement item in, even as exploratory, because I think it'll matter. On the upkeep question — you might be right that the comparison framing doesn't land for everyone, so maybe we test it as 'does this space look like it's being taken care of' and just drop the cross-neighborhood comparison. Simpler, and the cognitive interviews will tell us if residents are still reading something meaningful into it. But actually, before we wrap, there's one thing I want to flag that we haven't touched on yet, and I don't want it to get lost. Everything we've been doing is on the green space side — the exposure definition — and that's great, we've made real progress there. But I'm carrying a similar concern about the outcome side. 'Depression' and 'anxiety' as we're measuring them — the PHQ-9, the GAD-7, whatever we're planning to use — those instruments were developed and validated primarily on clinical populations that don't look much like the communities we're working in. And I'm not saying we should throw them out, because I know you need consistent, comparable measures. But I want us to at least have a conversation about what the qualitative arm is going to do with experiences that don't map neatly onto those scales. Like — chronic stress from housing precarity, from exposure to environmental hazards, from the kind of low-level constant vigilance that living in a disinvested neighborhood produces — residents might describe all of that in ways that don't register as 'anxiety' on a seven-item scale. If we're not attentive to that, we might systematically undercount distress in exactly the population we're trying to study. So — can we put that on the agenda? It doesn't have to be today, but I don't want us to get through IRB and into the field with that question unresolved.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Yeah — no, you're right, and I don't want to just defer that to 'after IRB' either, because that's how it becomes something we never actually resolve. So let me say clearly: I share that concern. I've been sitting with it for a while and I haven't fully worked out what to do about it methodologically. The PHQ-9 and GAD-7 are the best validated tools I have for producing numbers I can compare across participants and link to other studies, and dropping them would make the study almost impossible to situate in the existing literature. But — and this is the part that bothers me — they were built to detect clinical depression and clinical anxiety in populations where those categories mean something specific. In a community where someone is dealing with, like, constant low-grade dread about whether they can make rent, or hypervigilance because of neighborhood violence, some of that might show up on the scale and some of it might not. And if it doesn't, I'm not measuring what I think I'm measuring. So here's what I'd want to think through: the qualitative arm, can it be designed explicitly to capture what the PHQ-9 is probably missing? Like, not just 'tell us about your experience of the park' but also 'tell us what stress and worry actually look like in your day-to-day life' — and then we use that material to interrogate the quantitative findings, not just illustrate them. If the qualitative data shows forms of distress that don't register on the scale, that's a finding. That's us saying something honest about the limits of the instrument in this context. Does that feel like a direction you could work with? Because I need the PHQ-9 in there, but I want us to be more than defensive about it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: Yes — that's exactly the direction I want to go, and I'm genuinely glad you're framing it that way, because what you just described is actually a methodological contribution in itself. Using the qualitative arm to interrogate the quantitative instrument rather than just illustrate it — that's not a consolation prize for not having a better scale, that's a finding. And that reframe matters for how we write this up eventually. So yes, I can absolutely work with that. What I'd want to add is that when we design the qualitative interview guide, we're explicit with ourselves — and maybe in the methods write-up — that we're treating the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 as hypotheses about what distress looks like, not as transparent windows onto it. And then the qualitative material either confirms, or complicates, or partially challenges that hypothesis. That's defensible, it's honest, and it actually makes the mixed-methods design do something more interesting than just triangulating. The one concrete thing I'd suggest for the interview guide is that we don't use the clinical language — we don't ask about depression or anxiety by name, because those words carry their own framing that might not match how residents talk about their experience. We ask about what's weighing on them, what makes it hard to get through the week, what they're managing that other people might not see. And then we sit with whatever comes back and ask whether the PHQ-9 would have caught that or not. That comparison, done systematically across interviews, is the analysis. Does that feel like something you could sketch into the qualitative protocol alongside the park access questions? Because if we can get the basic structure of that into the IRB submission, even at a high level, we've at least signaled that this is part of the design intention and not an afterthought.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Yeah, I think we can do that — and honestly framing it as 'treating the PHQ-9 as a hypothesis' is language I can actually use in the methods section. That's useful. So let me think out loud about what that looks like in the IRB submission. I think what I'd want to write is something like: the quantitative arm uses validated screening instruments to capture depression and anxiety symptom burden, and the qualitative arm is designed to assess whether and how community-specific expressions of distress map onto those instruments — with the explicit intent of examining discordance, not just convergence. That signals to a reviewer that we know what we're doing and we're being deliberate about it, without me having to argue that the PHQ-9 is the wrong tool. Because I can't really make that argument and still have a defensible primary outcome measure. What I can do is be honest about the instrument's limits and design around them. On the language point — yes, I agree, we don't use 'depression' or 'anxiety' in the qualitative guide. We ask about weight, about managing, about what's hard. That's also just better interviewing practice in this context. So if you're willing to take a first pass at the qualitative interview structure — the park access questions we've already mapped out, plus this distress framing — I'll integrate it with the quantitative instrument write-up before I send anything to IRB. The thing I want to flag is timing: I need a rough structure from you by the same deadline as the cognitive interview protocol, end of next week, otherwise I'm writing the IRB narrative around a gap. Can you do both, or should we split the drafting differently?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: Yeah, I can do both by end of next week — it's a lot but I'd rather hold that deadline than have you writing around a gap. So let's say I draft the qualitative interview structure, park access questions and the distress framing together, and you get it alongside the cognitive interview protocol. And actually, I think they should be one document, not two, because the logic connecting them is the same — we're using resident accounts to stress-test our categorical assumptions, whether the category is 'park access' or 'anxiety.' If the IRB reviewer sees that as a coherent strategy running through the whole qualitative arm, that's a stronger submission. One thing I want to flag as I sit down to write it — and this is something that'll shape the framing in the IRB narrative — is that we should be explicit about why we're doing it this way, not just what we're doing. Like, the reason we're not asking 'do you feel anxious' and the reason we're not just counting meters to the park is the same reason: the standard categories were built somewhere else, for someone else, and we're working in a context where that matters. I can write that into the qualitative methods rationale in plain language, not as a theoretical detour, just as an honest statement of why the design looks the way it does. I think that actually strengthens the submission rather than opening us up to reviewer pushback — because a reviewer who asks 'why didn't you just use the standard protocol' deserves an answer, and we have a good one. Does that framing land for you, or do you want to see it before we commit to it?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Renata Osei
transcript.text: Yeah, that framing lands for me — and I think you're right that we're better off putting it in the narrative than leaving a reviewer to wonder. The one thing I'd want us to be careful about is tone. Like, there's a version of that rationale that reads as a critique of the whole field, and that's probably not what we want in an IRB submission. What I'd want is something more like: given the specific population and context, we designed the qualitative arm to examine the fit between standard instruments and community-expressed experience — something that signals methodological awareness without sounding like we're apologizing for using the PHQ-9 or picking a fight with psychometrics. So when you draft it, maybe lean toward 'contextual adaptation' framing rather than 'the standard categories were built for someone else' framing. Same idea, less likely to raise flags. Okay — I think we've actually landed on a real plan today, which I wasn't sure we would. Let me just say back what I think we've agreed on so we're both leaving with the same list. We're adding seven items on felt access alongside the time-spent measure. We're running six cognitive interviews before submission, with a two-out-of-six rewrite threshold. We're treating those access items as separate moderators in the primary analysis. We're keeping the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 as the outcome measures, and we're building the qualitative arm explicitly to probe what those scales might be missing. You're drafting both the cognitive interview protocol and the qualitative interview structure by end of next week as one integrated document, and I'll build the IRB narrative around that. Is there anything I'm missing or anything you'd push back on before we close?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lind
transcript.text: No, that summary is accurate — I'd sign off on all of it.
